claim_verdicts.evidence: kestrel.md (moniker >= aspnetcore-10.0): "Kestrel is the recommended server for ASP.NET Core, and it's configured by default in ASP.NET Core project templates." — recommended/default, not universal. servers/index.md lists the alternatives: "IIS HTTP Server is an in-process server for IIS.", "HTTP.sys server is a Windows-only HTTP server based on the HTTP.sys kernel driver", and under Hosting models: "HTTP.sys self-hosting is an alternative to Kestrel." With IIS in-process hosting the app runs "In the same process as the IIS worker process ... with the IIS HTTP Server", i.e. not on Kestrel.
claim_verdicts.suggested_text: Kestrel is the default web server for ASP.NET Core apps — the one project templates configure and the one Đơn Hàng will run on.

claim_verdicts.evidence: servers/index.md: "The server implementation listens for HTTP requests and surfaces them to the app as a set of request features composed into an HttpContext." — the bytes-to-request-object half is right. But TCP is not the only transport: kestrel.md lists "HTTP/1.1, HTTP/2 and HTTP/3"; http3.md: "`HTTP/3` uses QUIC instead of TCP." endpoints.md also documents ListenUnixSocket and "Customize Kestrel named pipe endpoints". So "a TCP connection" holds for the HTTP/1.1 traffic this lab uses, not for Kestrel in general.
claim_verdicts.suggested_text: it turns the bytes arriving on a connection — a TCP connection for the HTTP/1.1 traffic in this course — into a request your C# code can read, and turns your code's decision back into response bytes.

claim_verdicts.evidence: servers/index.md: "An ASP.NET Core app runs with an in-process HTTP server implementation. The server implementation listens for HTTP requests and surfaces them to the app as a set of request features composed into an HttpContext." Listening plus surfacing an HttpContext is the whole described responsibility; routing and business logic belong to the app/middleware above it (kestrel.md lists "Integration with ASP.NET Core: Seamless integration with other ASP.NET Core components, such as the middleware pipeline").

`git -C examples/don-hang show stage-0:Caddyfile` lines 36-40: `handle @postOrder {` / `header Content-Type "application/json; charset=utf-8"` / `header Location "/api/v1/orders/13"` / "respond `{\"id\":13,\"customer_id\":1,\"status\":\"new\"}` 201". Matcher at lines 14-17: `@postOrder { method POST  path /api/v1/orders }`. Body and status are literals in the config, so every matching request gets them.

`git -C examples/don-hang show stage-0:Caddyfile` lines 41-44: `handle @getOrder {` / `header Content-Type "application/json; charset=utf-8"` / "respond `{\"id\":1,\"customer_id\":1,\"status\":\"paid\"}` 200". Matcher lines 18-21: `@getOrder { method GET  path /api/v1/orders/1 }`. Confirmed by outputs/stage-0/scripts/http/methods.txt, which prints the same body twice for two GETs.
claim_verdicts.source: examples/don-hang Caddyfile @ stage-0, lines 18-21 and 41-44; outputs/stage-0/scripts/http/methods.txt

claim_verdicts.evidence: Caddy docs, respond directive: "<body> is the response body to write." Nothing there promises a constant body. Caddyfile Concepts states placeholders may be used as "arguments to directives and subdirectives" ("not all config fields support placeholders, but most do where you would expect it"), so a respond body can vary per request. The constancy in Đơn Hàng comes from the literal string in this Caddyfile, not from the directive itself.
claim_verdicts.suggested_text: In the stage-0 Caddyfile, each respond line's body is a literal string, so every matching request gets that same body back.

claim_verdicts.evidence: examples/don-hang outputs/stage-0/scripts/http/methods.txt @ stage-0 contains: "POST creates, so it also says where the new thing lives:" / "HTTP/1.1 201 Created" / "Location: /api/v1/orders/13". scripts/http/methods.sh pipes the POST response through `grep -Ei '^(HTTP/|Location:)'`, and the Caddyfile sets `header Location "/api/v1/orders/13"` as a literal, so the value cannot differ between runs.
claim_verdicts.source: examples/don-hang outputs/stage-0/scripts/http/methods.txt, scripts/http/methods.sh, Caddyfile line 38 @ stage-0

claim_verdicts.evidence: servers/index.md: "An ASP.NET Core app runs with an in-process HTTP server implementation." kestrel/when-to-use-a-reverse-proxy.md attributes load spreading to the proxy in front, not to Kestrel: "A reverse proxy server receives HTTP requests from the network and forwards them to Kestrel" and "A reverse proxy: ... Simplifies load balancing and secure communication (HTTPS) configuration."

servers/index.md: "The server implementation listens for HTTP requests and surfaces them to the app as a set of request features composed into an HttpContext" — surfacing an HttpContext is work beyond accepting a socket. kestrel.md documents the protocol work explicitly: "Wide protocol support: Kestrel supports common web protocols, including: HTTP/1.1, HTTP/2 and HTTP/3 ... WebSockets". Accepting a connection alone yields none of that.

issues.quote: **Kestrel** — the web server every ASP.NET Core app runs on
issues.text: "every ASP.NET Core app" is contradicted by the docs for the pinned 10.0 version: with IIS in-process hosting the server is IIS HTTP Server, and HTTP.sys self-hosting is "an alternative to Kestrel". kestrel.md only says Kestrel is "the recommended server for ASP.NET Core, and it's configured by default in ASP.NET Core project templates". The same absolute appears in Five-line summary line 1.
issues.fix: Replace both occurrences with the default framing, e.g. "the default web server for ASP.NET Core apps — the one project templates configure and the one Đơn Hàng will run on" (Core concepts) and "Kestrel is the default web server for ASP.NET Core apps, turning connection bytes into a request object …" (summary line 1). Update claim 1 in .meta.json to match.

issues.quote: it is copied verbatim from the `Caddyfile` on every request, exactly like `www/index.html` is.
issues.text: Unlisted claim: as written, this says `www/index.html` is also copied verbatim from the `Caddyfile`. It is not — at stage-0 Caddy serves it with `root * /srv/www` plus `file_server`, i.e. read from disk; only the `respond` body lives in the Caddyfile. No claim in the ledger covers how the static file is served.
issues.fix: Rewrite as: "The id never changes because the response is not computed: it is copied verbatim from the `Caddyfile` on every request, the same way `www/index.html` is copied verbatim off disk." Add it as a claim in .meta.json (kind behavior, source examples/don-hang Caddyfile @ stage-0, `root * /srv/www` + `file_server`).

issues.quote: it turns bytes arriving on a TCP connection into a request your C# code can read
issues.text: Stated without condition, this is false for part of Kestrel 10.0: HTTP/3 runs over QUIC, not TCP ("`HTTP/3` uses QUIC instead of TCP"), and Kestrel can also listen on Unix sockets (ListenUnixSocket) and named pipes. The statement is true of the HTTP/1.1 traffic this course uses, but the lesson does not say so.
issues.fix: Add the condition once, in Core concepts: "…bytes arriving on a connection — a TCP connection for the HTTP/1.1 traffic in this course — into a request your C# code can read." No change needed in the diagram or quiz, which are explicitly about this lab's traffic.

issues.quote: `respond` is Caddy's word for "send exactly this, every time."
issues.text: Too strong as a statement about the directive. Caddy docs define only "<body> is the response body to write", and Caddyfile Concepts allows placeholders as "arguments to directives and subdirectives", so a `respond` body can vary per request. What is fixed here is the literal string in this Caddyfile, not `respond` itself.
issues.fix: Rewrite as: "Both bodies here are literal strings typed into `Caddyfile`, so `respond` sends exactly that text back on every matching request." Adjust claim 6 in .meta.json the same way.

issues.quote: Kestrel is the process that will claim Đơn Hàng's.
issues.text: Kestrel is not a process; the docs call it an "in-process HTTP server implementation", and the lesson itself says so in Beginners often think ("Kestrel is the server running inside one app process"). Section 1 contradicts section 6 on the lesson's own core concept.
issues.fix: Rewrite as: "…Kestrel, running inside the Đơn Hàng app process, is what will claim its port."

issues.quote: how your future ASP.NET Core code will ever get a chance to run at all
issues.text: "ASP.NET Core" is never explained, and the Core concepts entry defines the one new term with it: "the web server every ASP.NET Core app runs on". So the definition of Kestrel rests on a term I do not have. I guess it means "a C# web app", and the guess carries me through the whole lesson.
issues.fix: At the first mention in section 2, add a six-word gloss in plain words: "your future ASP.NET Core code (the C# way of writing web apps in this course)", and keep using that reading in Core concepts.

issues.quote: every request to `/api/v1/orders` today gets the same fixed JSON back from Caddy
issues.text: Caddy and `Caddyfile` appear in the opening sentence as if I had already met them; neither prerequisite summary mentions either. I only learn Caddy is a web server later, in Core concepts, and I am never told `Caddyfile` is the file that tells Caddy what to do.
issues.fix: In section 2, at the first mention, write "…back from Caddy, the web server running in the lab, whose whole behaviour is written in one text file, `Caddyfile`" — one clause, placed before the file is opened.

issues.quote: You are ready to build the real Đơn Hàng order API

issues.text: "stage-0" is used several times, plus `tag=stage-0` in the code fence header, and is never explained. I cannot tell whether it is a folder, a version of the lab, or a marker in the repository, so in Try it I do not know which files I am supposed to be looking at.

skipped_steps: "You notice this when someone expects one Kestrel to survive its own machine going down." — nothing links load spreading to a machine failing.
"an incoming request reaches a method that runs fresh each time" — where the method comes from is never said here.
The code block's `handle @postOrder` line and `header Location` line are never mentioned in the prose, which explains only `respond`.
